assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, reach fractional uncertainties near 10^-18 and turn atomic spectroscopy into a tool for fundamental physics: tests of constant variation, relativistic redshift across millimetres, and a route to redefining the second. This is the kind of precision measurement where theory and experiment agree quantitatively, and it opens genuinely new questions about time and gravity.
assessment.attribution: Katori conceived the magic-wavelength lattice scheme and demonstrated the first Sr lattice clock; Ye's JILA group pushed it to the 10^-18 regime and to many-body (spin-exchange) clock physics. Two laureates give a clean and defensible configuration; the trapped-ion (Wineland) and Hall/Hansch comb contributions were already recognised.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and others) have reproduced and surpassed each other's results over about twenty years; the interpretation is stable and the field is mature, so recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Whether the committee wishes to treat this as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes on frequency combs and ion control.
Relative credit for early lattice-clock ideas (Katori, Ye, and the earlier Ye and Lemonde contributions) is not fully settled in the supplied text; I rely on memory rather than verification.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Trapping and cooling antihydrogen and measuring it spectroscopically (1S-2S, hyperfine structure, gravitational response) and the antiproton and positron magnetic moments probe CPT symmetry and matter-antimatter asymmetry at extraordinary precision. It asks a fundamental question about nature, with a clear and unexpected experimental achievement.
assessment.attribution: Gabrielse led the ATRAP effort and the single-particle antiproton and electron g-factor measurements; Hangst leads ALPHA, which trapped and spectroscopically probed antihydrogen. Credit is split across large collaborations and the competing ATRAP and ALPHA teams, and others such as Wolfgang Ketterle-era cooling or Rolf Landua/ATHENA are not available in the supplied names; the two-person configuration is reasonable but contestable.
assessment.maturity: ALPHA, ATRAP and ASACUSA have independently confirmed key results, and the 1S-2S line is now measured to about 10^-12. The programme is still advancing, so some results (gravity, further CPT tests) are maturing rather than final.
uncertainties: No violation of CPT has been seen, so the prize would rest on the technique and measurement rather than on a surprising result.
Treatment of the ATHENA and ATRAP competition and of Gabrielse's separate electron g-2 work could complicate the configuration.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The observation of the Higgs boson at 125 GeV in 2012 completed the Standard Model and confirmed the mechanism recognised by the 2013 prize. It is an unambiguous, enormously consequential discovery. I defer to colleagues on particle physics, but its importance and clarity are hard to dispute.
assessment.attribution: A prize to the experiments must confront the limit of three persons against two collaborations of thousands. Gianotti and Virdee as spokespersons at the time of discovery are the most natural individual names in this list, but Della Negra and Jenni, as founders and early leaders, also have strong claims; no choice is fully fair.
assessment.maturity: Independent confirmation by ATLAS and CMS, the Tevatron evidence and the later coupling measurements make the discovery very mature, and the delay since 2012 raises the awkwardness of waiting.
uncertainties: Attribution to individuals rather than collaborations is the central unresolved problem.
I rely on particle-physics colleagues to judge who contributed decisively, as that is outside my own field.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The recollision model explains high-harmonic generation and the plateau and cutoff law physically in terms of an ionised electron driven back to its parent ion. It is the intellectual foundation of attosecond science, which I know well: it supplies the simple picture that experiments and my own time-delay calculations are interpreted through.
assessment.attribution: Corkum's semiclassical three-step model and the Kulander-Schafer simulations and Lewenstein's quantum strong-field approximation derivation are the core contributions. Kulander's death and the overlap with the 2023 laureates (Agostini, Krausz, L'Huillier) complicate any new configuration; Corkum alone could be the cleanest case, but three names are available.
assessment.maturity: The model has been tested widely and underlies high-harmonic spectroscopy and attosecond metrology, so it is extremely mature. The main issue is timing, since the committee honoured the experimental side in 2023.
uncertainties: The 2023 prize may be seen as having already recognised this area.
Because of my close ties to the attosecond community I should treat my judgement here with caution and expect to recuse or discount my own view.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Time-reversal-invariant topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect revealed a new class of quantum matter in which a bulk gap coexists with protected edge states. The experimental realisation in HgTe was a striking confirmation of a clear theoretical prediction.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the theoretical proposal and the Z2 classification; Molenkamp's group observed the quantum spin Hall edge transport in HgTe. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction for HgTe is not in the supplied credit, and Zhang is deceased, so the configuration omits an important contributor.
assessment.maturity: Many independent laboratories have confirmed topological insulator physics in 2D and 3D, and the field is mature, with the 2016 prize covering the earlier topological phases.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2016 Nobel prize and with Moore and Balents, Fu, Kane, and Zhang-group 3D topological insulator work.
Condensed-matter attribution is outside my own field and I defer to colleagues.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices simulate Hubbard-type models with controllable parameters, as shown by the observed Mott-insulator transition and by later single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopy. It joins atomic physics and many-body theory in a way that I find compelling.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch, Cirac) provided the theoretical proposals, while Greiner, Bloch and Esslinger provided the experiments. Dieter Jaksch is not in the credited list, and five credited names exceed the three-person limit, so the choice is difficult and somewhat arbitrary.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced in many laboratories and developed into quantum gas microscopes, but the original goals of quantum simulation of high-Tc physics are only partly achieved, so the case may be maturing.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2001 BEC prize and the 2012 prize for quantum control of single atoms and ions.
The most decisive set of three among five credited people is unclear.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed states of light beat the standard quantum limit in interferometry and are now used in gravitational-wave detectors. The idea connects quantum optics to a precision instrument that has already produced a Nobel-recognised discovery.
assessment.attribution: Caves supplied the 1981 theoretical proposal, Kimble's group made early experimental demonstrations of squeezing, and Schnabel led the GEO600 and later work. Slusher and others who first observed squeezing, and Mavalvala, are not all included; credit is spread over many contributors.
assessment.maturity: Implemented in GEO600 and LIGO and Virgo with demonstrated sensitivity gains, which is strong confirmation; the interpretation is stable.
uncertainties: The first experimental observation (Slusher et al.) is not among the proposed names, which weakens a clean attribution.
The 2017 gravitational-wave prize may be seen as already covering the main impact.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Programmable arrays of optical tweezers loaded with single atoms and coupled through Rydberg interactions provide a platform for quantum simulation and computation. I like it as atomic physics with controllable many-body interactions, though it is more recent and technology-oriented.
assessment.attribution: Saffman and colleagues proposed Rydberg-blockade gates, Browaeys and Lukin demonstrated entanglement and programmable arrays; the Bernien and Endres-type work and Jaksch, Cirac and Zoller proposals are not in the credited list, so the allocation is uncertain.
assessment.maturity: Several groups have reproduced the key results, but the field is still developing rapidly and the long-term interpretation as a computing platform is not yet settled, so recognition may be premature.
uncertainties: Premature relative to the pace of the field.
Credit among Lukin, Browaeys, Saffman and the omitted pioneers is unresolved.
